metadata.title: Who can log in? The importance of skills for the feasibility of teleworking arrangements across OECD countries (EN)
metadata.venue: OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses microdata from the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) first cycle, drawing on respondents aged 18–64 from three data-collection rounds conducted between 2011 and 2017. The paper constructs a binary “telework” feasibility indicator from 12 PIAAC task/frequency questions across three domains (physical skills, job flexibility, and ICT/reading/writing intensity), and then reports feasibility shares by education, PIAAC literacy/numeracy proficiency levels, income quintiles, and occupation (ISCO 2008 2-digit). The manuscript does not report the specific use of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures; therefore, analysts should consult the PIAAC technical documentation for the appropriate sampling weights when reproducing population-representative estimates. Because the analysis is based on OECD/PIAAC survey microdata and produces cross-country shares, weighting is typically important for correct standard errors and population inference, even though the paper itself does not specify weight variable names.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a constructed binary feasibility indicator (“telework” = 1 if the job is judged compatible with telework, 0 otherwise) derived from questionnaire responses about task requirements and their frequency. Plausible Values (PV) are typically used for cognitive achievement scales in ILSA, but this paper’s main outcome is not reported as a PV-based achievement score. The paper also does not describe a missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case selection or imputation), which is a reporting gap for replication.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PIAAC first-cycle microdata for respondents aged 18–64, with data collected in three rounds between 2011 and 2017. Telework feasibility is constructed from 12 PIAAC questions spanning three domains (physical skills, job flexibility, and ICT/reading/writing intensity), and the resulting binary telework indicator is used for cross-country comparisons. The paper states that the Russian Federation estimate excludes the population of the Moscow municipal area (i.e., the sample does not represent the entire resident population aged 16–65 in Russia). Beyond this, the manuscript does not specify additional analytic exclusions (e.g., missingness rules, item nonresponse handling, or further subsample restrictions).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PIAAC first-cycle adult skills microdata (respondents aged 18–64; data collected in three rounds between 2011 and 2017) from 38 countries to estimate the feasibility of teleworking in theory. The authors construct a binary “telework” indicator from 12 PIAAC questions across three domains: physical skills, job flexibility, and the intensity of ICT/reading/writing skills in workplaces. They report that about 31% of OECD workers could, in theory, work from home, with substantial cross-country variation and robustness checks via upper and lower bound specifications. Feasibility is strongly patterned by education (54% for tertiary-educated vs 18% without tertiary education) and by skills proficiency (literacy Level 4–5: ~57% vs Level 3 and below: ~28%; similar patterns for numeracy). The paper further shows large gaps by income quintiles (top 20%: ~56% vs bottom 20%: ~14%) and highlights that even after controlling for observed characteristics in a probit framework, higher-skilled workers are roughly twice as likely to be telework-compatible. The implication is that pandemic-era teleworking capacity may exacerbate labour-market inequalities, especially for lower-skilled and less-educated groups, though the study focuses on feasibility rather than actual telework uptake.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper that primarily performs descriptive and regression-based estimation of a constructed feasibility indicator rather than training and evaluating machine-learning predictive models. As a result, there are no ML techniques to extract, no PV-based achievement outcome to map, and no student-level ML performance metrics to report. The paper also does not provide a complete analytic-sample size (total N) or per-country N in the provided text, so the sample-size fields remain sparse by design and reporting.
